source.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
source.authors: Bo Gong; Shiyang Lai; James Evans; D. Song

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE-based feature and neuron measurements to language models rather than toy networks, reporting results about polysemantic structure and interference in those models.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition for background but does not reproduce its toy-network experiments. Results from cited work are not recorded. Figures 7 and 17 show distributions without extractable per-layer numbers; they are recorded as figure-only. Intervention-strength choices and prompt-generation instructions are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Neuronpedia SAEs on Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small as a tool. It treats SAE decoder directions as features and superposition as background, then reports how well its own interventions (SAE direction, token gradient, prompt injection, neuron masking/amplification) shift next-token distributions and transfer to larger models. It never tests whether features are superposed, whether SAEs recover the model's features, or whether features are spread across neurons. Its descriptive statistics (active-feature counts, interference distributions, neuron–feature connection counts) are setup measurements derived from the SAE, not tests of any version. The core results are steering effects on a related construct, interference-based vulnerability, so they belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that interfering but semantically unrelated features, found via SAEs in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small, can steer next-token outputs through SAE-direction, token-gradient and prompt interventions. Patterns shared by the two small models transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for some target types. Most shared interference pairs (over 70%) lack human-intelligible relations. Neuron output sensitivity rises with polysemanticity, with asymmetric effects for super-neurons. They argue polysemanticity is structured and convergent rather than incidental.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained SAEs, feature-direction and token-gradient steering, prompt injection, and neuron interventions in language models; it does not reproduce the original toy-network optimization or its sparsity and geometry sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects differ by model and intervention method: SAE-direction steering is weaker on GPT-2-Small than Pythia-70M; token-gradient steering is reported as roughly 10× stronger than SAE-direction steering; prompt injection is weaker than direct latent-space manipulation for the weighted-cosine metric. Neuron effects differ between suppression and amplification, especially for super-neurons. The authors also report sensitivity to evaluation metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering along SAE directions, or along their token gradients, that are semantically unrelated but have high decoder cosine with a target shifts next-token predictions toward the target. The effect is larger at higher interference for SAE directions and about 10× larger with token gradients. Shared interference tokens from the small models transfer to Llama-3.1-8B/70B and Gemma-2-9B for some target types (location, number, science) but not others.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cosine overlap between SAE feature directions (interference) predicts cross-feature steering effects on outputs, and some interference patterns are shared across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons connected to more SAE feature clusters have larger output effects when masked or amplified. 'Super-neurons' (>500 features) show small masking effects but very large amplification effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron polysemanticity, as measured by SAE connections, correlates with how sensitive outputs are to manipulating that neuron, with asymmetric effects for hub neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Only 27.7% of high-interference, low-similarity shared pairs are judged by an LLM annotator to have a higher-order semantic link. In a matched paired choice, high-interference pairs were picked as more related 64.3% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interference among SAE features in small LMs is only weakly aligned with human-interpretable semantic relations.

record.problems: The main evidence relies on SAE feature interpretations and immediate next-token probability shifts; the authors note SAE feature instability, limited intervention depth, and limited transferability robustness testing. Larger-model internal SAE recovery and substantial downstream behavior are not established here. Several distributions are shown only in figures without extractable numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature/dimension or sparsity sweep, no geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition or feature importance.
No test of non-capacity origins of polysemanticity. The authors only argue that cross-model transfer challenges the 'incidental artifact' view.
SAE recovery and spread of features across neurons are assumed, not tested.
SAE completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested. SAE instability is acknowledged via citations.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Distribution of pairwise interference (decoder cosine) between SAE features. Pythia Res-4: 85.5% below 0.1; GPT-2 Res Post-4: 95.6% below 0.15. Positive but weak association with semantic similarity. This is near-orthogonality of SAE directions, a descriptive statistic of the SAE.
missing.versions: none (descriptive SAE statistic; possibly relevant context for V4)

missing.what: Prompt-injection transfer success rates to larger models by target type, compared with a random baseline.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V4 labels are rejected. The paper uses SAEs as a tool and does not assess whether SAE recovery or feature spread holds. The <5% figure in r3/r4 was misread. The authors' claim that transfer challenges the 'incidental artifact' account (Lecomte et al.) touches V3 only by argument, not by a test of the origins of polysemanticity. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment, explicit feature-count-to-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular-geometry test.
Does not test capacity competition, feature importance, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from mechanisms other than capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.

Does not validate SAE completeness or recovery fidelity, and does not establish that features are broadly distributed across neurons in larger models. The SAE-based structural measurements are on Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across training choices, or canonical units. Discussion of SAE instability cites prior work.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multi-dimensional features.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Counted neurons strongly connected to aggregated SAE feature clusters, using connection strength greater than 0.2.
rows.measure: Share of neurons strongly connected to aggregated features that are polysemantic
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in figure; numeric intervals not stated
rows.locator: Appendix N, Figure 17A; Appendix N text
rows.note: The paper reports a small share of strongly connected polysemantic neurons; the figure does not provide extractable layer-specific values.
rows.check: Value is misparaphrased. Appendix N says strongly connected polysemantic neurons are under 5% of neurons per layer. Sec 3.6 says neurons linked to 1–2 aggregated features are over 33% of strongly connected neurons. The record's 'share among strongly connected neurons' reading is not supported. The counts also depend on SAE clustering and a 0.2 threshold, so they do not measure feature spread across neurons as V4 names it.

rows.measure: Relative change in weighted cosine similarity toward the target feature
rows.baseline: Random feature intervention and target-feature intervention are shown as references.
rows.value: The text reports reliable steering; stronger effects at higher interference levels.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in figure; regression reports p < 0.001, but coefficients are not unambiguously assignable from the flattened figure text.
rows.note: The paper reports that semantically dissimilar interfering SAE directions alter target-feature output probabilities. It does not provide extractable bar values in the text.
rows.check: This is a steering effect of interfering SAE directions on next-token outputs. It does not show that the model contains sparse features an SAE recovers; it assumes this. The effect is real for the study's own construct, so it belongs in fits_no_version, not V4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE-derived feature-direction interventions in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that interventions using semantically distinct but interfering SAE feature directions reliably shift target-feature outputs; the effect is weaker in GPT-2-Small (r5–r6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Strong neuron-feature connections in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small
reader_labels.reason: The reported share of strongly connected neurons classified as polysemantic is fewer than 5% in each layer, so the evidence does not show widespread polysemanticity across neurons (r3–r4).
